items.title: Define the built-in command scanner's supported security contract

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

items.body:
**What problem would this solve?**

The optional built-in command scanner uses finite command patterns to request approval. Its supported command families, shell dialects and threshold behavior need a clear maintenance contract so users understand what protection it provides and contributors know which changes belong in core.

**What would a good outcome look like?**

Should Goose continue bounded command-pattern expansion as an approval safeguard, adopt a bounded parser/control for specified dialects, or de-emphasize this scanner in favor of explicitly advisory behavior and external controls?

**Possible approaches**

Define supported command families and platforms, semantic-equivalent syntax, legitimate-operation negatives, effective approval thresholds and behavior for unsupported syntax. Preserve ordinary tool permissions and existing positive detections until a change is explicitly agreed. Any approval-policy change must behave consistently in both agent loops.

**Additional context**

This concerns the existing built-in scanner, not loading third-party rule packs into core. The external plugin/hook boundary agreed in #9126 remains unchanged. Classifier availability and outage behavior are separately discussed in #12144. Verification should use inert command strings and captured approval decisions; it should not execute destructive commands or imply exhaustive shell protection.

- [x] I have verified this does not duplicate an existing feature request

Do not begin implementation until the issue reaches **Ready** on the [Goose Issues board](https://github.com/orgs/aaif-goose/projects/1).

items.title: Define destructive disk-write detection across shell I/O forms

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

items.body:
**What problem would this solve?**

The optional shell security scanner recognizes destructive disk writes only when both source and destination are expressed as explicit operands in one order. Standard input, standard output, pipelines, and redirections can represent the same disk-write intent but receive different approval treatment. Device naming also varies across platforms.

**What would a good outcome look like?**

Equivalent destructive raw-device writes are classified consistently across supported shell and command forms, with clear platform coverage and predictable false-positive behavior.

**Possible approaches**

Define operand, redirection, pipeline, command-boundary, device-namespace, and dialect semantics; parse shell structure before classification; or replace narrow command matching with a conservative structured raw-device-write policy.

**Additional context**

Tests should cover equivalent I/O forms, benign file copies, multiple command boundaries, and supported device families.

- [x] I have verified this does not duplicate an existing feature request

Do not begin implementation until the issue reaches **Ready** on the [Goose Issues board](https://github.com/orgs/aaif-goose/projects/1).

items.title: Subagents cannot be resumed after failure/interruption; parent re-delegates the same work from scratch
items.body:
**Describe the bug**

Subagent sessions cannot be continued once they fail or get interrupted:

1. **A failed subagent cannot be continued.** When a delegated subagent fails (provider error, max turns, etc.), the parent agent receives only the failure reason (`Subagent <id> failed: max turns reached; last response: ...`) and the subagent session is permanently marked as delivered — it will never run again. The only lever the parent LLM has is calling `delegate` again, which always creates a **brand-new session** and repeats the whole task from scratch, even though the failed subagent's partial transcript is still persisted in session storage.

2. **An interrupted subagent cannot be resumed either.** If the user interrupts the parent while a foreground subagent is running, the subagent is aborted and recorded as "cancelled before it finished and will not run again". The partial work is preserved on disk but is unreachable programmatically.

Impact: wasted tokens and wall-clock time on re-delegation, and repeated (potentially destructive) side effects when a long task restarts from step one.

---

**To Reproduce**

Path A (max turns failure → full re-run):
1. Ask the lead agent to delegate a multi-step task with a small turn budget, e.g.: "delegate a subagent with max_turns: 1 to research X and write a summary to out.md".
2. The subagent hits the turn limit; the parent receives `Subagent <id> failed: max turns reached...`.
3. Ask the parent to get the task done. It calls `delegate` with the same instructions → a new subagent session starts from scratch; none of the previous partial work (context, findings, disk progress) carries over.

Path B (interrupt → permanent cancel):
1. Delegate a long-running task and press Esc while the subagent is running.
2. The subagent is reported as "cancelled before it finished and will not run again". Its session with partial progress remains in storage, but no tool can resume it.

---

**Expected behavior**

- The parent (and/or the user) can **resume** a failed/cancelled subagent session, e.g. `delegate(resume: <subagent_session_id>, message: "continue", extra_turns: N)`, so work continues from the persisted transcript instead of restarting.

---

**Root cause (main branch source analysis)**

- `crates/goose/src/agents/platform_extensions/summon.rs` — the `delegate` tool schema has no resume/stop parameters, and `handle_foreground_delegate` always creates a new child session.
- `crates/goose/src/agents/subagent_handler.rs` — `SubagentOutcome::Failed` is delivered once; only sessions that already saved a successful `final_output` are resumed idempotently on the parent's next turn (that path works well). Failed ones are never re-run.
- `crates/goose/src/agents/state_machine/ops_foreground_subagent.rs` — cancelled subagents are annotated "will not run again"; delivered/cancelled annotations exclude them from `pending_subagents()`.
- Max-turns nuance: `ops_maxturns.rs` counts assistant turns since the kickoff message, and `messages_since_kickoff` (`crates/goose-agent/src/operation.rs`) slices from the **last** user-visible message. So merely re-running the same subagent session with the same limit would immediately re-hit the limit, while appending a user "continue" message to the subagent session would naturally reset the budget — a cheap building block for resume.

---

**Suggested fix directions**

1. Add a resume path: `delegate(resume: subagent_session_id, message?, extra_turns?)` (or a `resume_delegate` tool) reusing `ForegroundSubagentRunner::start`, plus a hint in the `delegate` tool description to prefer resume over re-spawning after a failure.
2. Include `subagent_session_id` and a transcript tail in the failure delivery so the parent can continue meaningfully even when re-delegating.

Related but separate: #12852 (messaging/soft-stopping a subagent *while it runs*) — split out of this issue.

---

**Please provide the following information**

- **OS & Arch:** Windows 10 x64
- **Interface:** UI (also verified against source; provider-agnostic)
- **Version:** 1.54.0 (analysis against current `main`)
- **Extensions enabled:** built-in developer/summon (delegate)
- **Provider & Model:** any

---

**Additional context**

The failed subagent's partial transcript is not lost — it persists as a `SubAgent`-type session — it is just not addressable by any tool. Workarounds we use today: instruct delegates to checkpoint progress to disk after each step (idempotent re-runs), and set generous `max_turns` upfront.

items.title: Per-chat actions (context menu) in the sidebar `CHATS` list — Pin, Rename, Archive, Delete

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

items.body:
**Summary**

Add a hover-activated **three-dots (⋯) context menu** to each session in the sidebar `CHATS` list, exposing quick per-chat actions **without** having to navigate to the separate `Session History` view. At minimum: **Rename, Pin, Archive, Delete**.

## Problem / Motivation

Today, session management actions are split across two surfaces, which is friction for a common, high-frequency task:

- **Sidebar `CHATS` list** (the ~10 most recent sessions): supports inline **rename via double-click**, but has **no delete, no pin, no archive**.
- **`Session History` view**: has hover **✏️ rename** and **🗑️ delete** on session cards — but reaching it is a detour from where I actually live day-to-day (the sidebar).

Two concrete gaps:

1. **No quick delete/manage from the sidebar** — I have to leave my current context and open `Session History` to clean up.
2. **No "Archive" concept anywhere in goose** — the only way to declutter the sidebar is *permanent* deletion. There's no non-destructive "hide this from the list but keep the record" option.

## Proposed Solution

On hover of a sidebar `CHATS` item, show a **⋯ menu** (and ideally an inline **pin** affordance). Menu items:

- **Pin / Star** — keep important chats at the top of the list, unaffected by recency.
- **Rename** — (already possible via double-click; include here for discoverability).
- **Archive** — remove from the active sidebar list **without deleting** the underlying session record. Add an **"Archived"** view/filter to browse and **restore** archived chats.
- **Delete** — existing permanent delete, surfaced in-context (with the current confirmation modal).

### Why "Archive" specifically
Delete is permanent and irreversible (it removes the local session record, and also from the CLI). Many chats aren't worth keeping in the active list but are also not worth destroying. Archive gives a safe middle ground and is the main net-new capability being requested here.

## Prior Art (other agent harnesses)

This pattern is well-established and sets user expectations:

- **Anthropic / Claude**: hover a chat → **⋯** menu with **Star, Rename, Add to project, Delete**.
- **OpenAI / ChatGPT**: hover a chat → inline **pin** icon + **⋯** menu with **Share, Rename, Archive, Delete** (and an "Archived chats" management view).

Bringing equivalent per-chat controls into the goose sidebar would close a visible UX gap versus these tools.

## Alternatives Considered

- **Keep actions only in `Session History`** — works, but adds navigation friction for a frequent task and still provides no archive.
- **Sidebar-only delete (no archive)** — helps, but doesn't solve the "declutter without losing" need.

## Additional Context

- Related (but distinct): #8140 — *Make sidebar session list limit configurable*. That addresses the **length** of the list; this request addresses **per-item actions** and adds **archive/pin**. They complement each other.
- Rename and delete already exist (rename: sidebar double-click + Session History hover-edit; delete: Session History hover-trash), so the primary net-new asks are **Archive** and **Pin**, plus **surfacing all actions in the sidebar context menu**.
- Platform: goose Desktop.

## Acceptance Criteria (suggested)

- [ ] Hovering a sidebar `CHATS` item reveals a ⋯ menu (keyboard-accessible).
- [ ] Menu includes Pin, Rename, Archive, Delete.
- [ ] Pinned chats stay at the top regardless of recency.
- [ ] Archiving hides a chat from the active list but preserves the record; an Archived view allows restore.
- [ ] Delete retains the existing confirmation + permanence semantics.

items.title: Switching model/provider mid-run swaps provider under active turn; should defer to next turn
items.body:
Before filing, please check common issues:
https://goose-docs.ai/docs/troubleshooting

Describe the bug

Switching model or provider from Desktop while a turn is still running swaps the live Agent provider immediately, mid-turn. The running turn can continue on the new provider with the old ModelConfig (legacy loop) or finish on stale state while the session already claims the new model. Result is a mixed-model turn: wrong capabilities, broken tool-call continuity, misleading cost and traces.

To Reproduce
1. Start a session in Desktop (ACP) and send a long-running prompt with many tool calls.
2. While status is Thinking or Streaming (chatState not Idle), open the model picker bottom bar and select a different model or provider.
3. Observe: change applies on the fly, current turn continues or changes behavior mid-run instead of waiting for the run to finish.

Expected behavior

The in-flight turn keeps its original provider and model. The selection applies to the next user message after the run finishes (deferred, not mid-turn). UI should indicate pending state such as will apply next turn rather than pretending it already switched. No auto-cancel of the run; user can explicitly Stop then resend if they want the new model now.

Screenshots
N/A

Please provide the following information
- OS and Arch: macOS arm64 (also applies cross-platform)
- Interface: UI (Desktop ACP)
- Version: 1.48.0
- Extensions enabled: any
- Provider and Model: any to any (repro with model-only switch and provider switch)

Additional context

Analysis:
- UI: ModelAndProviderContext changeModel calls acpSetSessionProviderModel in ui/desktop/src/acp/providers.ts which sends session setConfigOption for provider and model with no busy check. Picker stays enabled while chatState is not Idle (BaseChat).
- Server: dispatch.rs routes to server.rs on_set_model (line 2365) and update_provider (line 2482), then agent recreate_provider_for_session, then agent update_provider (agent.rs line 3414) which locks self.provider and swaps in the new provider plus persists session immediately.
- Legacy loop (reply): re-reads self.provider every LLM iteration but keeps model_config snapshotted at turn start, so new provider plus old model config mid-turn.
- State machine (GOOSE_STATE_MACHINE=1): create_state_machine snapshots provider and model at reply start, so current turn is more isolated, but session record and UI already claim the new model.
- Gate exists but unused: active_prompt_runs rejects a second prompt while busy, model change ignores it.

How others handle it:
- ChatGPT, Claude.ai, Claude Code: selector applies to next message, running stream is immutable.
- Cursor, Copilot Chat: run binds model at kickoff, dropdown is for next run, often disabled while busy.
- Aider, Continue: slash model command is between turns.
- Raw OpenAI and Anthropic APIs: single complete or stream call cannot change model mid-stream; agent wrappers do not swap between tool-loop iterations.
- Only explicit alternative is Stop and retry with new model, which is destructive and distinct from silent settings change.

Proposed scope for Ready discussion:
1. If session idle, apply immediately (todays behavior).
2. If active_prompt_runs has an active run, pin current turn to its provider and model snapshot; store pending selection; apply when run clears, before next queued or user message.
3. Do not apply new model on next LLM call inside same turn (still splits one job across models).
4. Desktop: keep picker usable but show pending next-turn state.
5. Do not auto-cancel. Must cover both agent.rs legacy path and state_machine path for parity.

Non-goals: auto-cancel-and-restart with new model; per-step model routing; changing global defaults mid-run.

Verification plan:
- Start long tool-loop run, switch model mid-run: assert all usage and inference in that run uses original model, session switches only after run end.
- Same for provider switch and thinking effort switch.
- Queued message after switch uses new model.
- UI test: picker during Streaming shows pending, then updates on Idle.
- cargo test -p goose ACP server tests plus state machine parity tests; pnpm typecheck and test for picker.

Do not begin implementation until the issue reaches Ready on the Goose Issues board.

items.title: OAuth credentials for streamable HTTP extensions erased by concurrent session starts — endless re-auth loop
items.body:
## Summary

Stored OAuth credentials for a streamable HTTP extension can be **erased by Goose itself** when multiple sessions start concurrently, producing an endless re-authentication loop: the user completes the vendor's browser auth, and within minutes/hours the browser window opens again. We reproduced this repeatedly with Miro's official MCP (`https://mcp.miro.com/`) on the pinned commit `2694fff7e`.

## Observed behavior (evidence)

Timeline from a single machine, **one goosed process running the entire time** (verified via `ps`):

1. `11:40` — user completes Miro browser auth. Keychain secrets blob (service `goose`, account `secrets`) contains a valid `oauth_creds_miro` entry (client_id + token_response). Verified by reading the blob.
2. `12:12–12:13` — a scheduled automation creates one ACP session plus two sub-agent sessions (session IDs `20260806_86/87/88` in sessions.db, created within 54s of each other). All three eagerly connect enabled extensions, including `miro` (confirmed via the sessions' stored `enabled_extensions.v0` extension_data).
3. `12:14` — the Miro auth page opens in the browser again. The keychain secrets blob now reads `{}` — **all stored OAuth credentials gone**.

This loop repeats on every concurrent-session event. The user in question completed Miro auth 3+ times over two days.

## Mechanism (verified in source at `2694fff7e`)

1. **Every auth-required connect forces a refresh.** `crates/goose/src/oauth/mod.rs` (`oauth_flow`, ~line 93): when `initialize_from_store()` finds stored credentials, it *unconditionally* calls `refresh_token()` — regardless of token expiry.
2. **Any refresh failure erases stored credentials.** Same function (~lines 98–108): on any `refresh_token()` error it calls `credential_store.clear()` and falls back to browser auth. A second clear path exists in `crates/goose/src/agents/extension_manager.rs` (`clear_credentials_on_post_refresh_auth_failure`).
3. **Concurrent connections don't coordinate.** Each session's connection builds its own `AuthorizationManager` + `GooseCredentialStore` (`crates/goose/src/oauth/persist.rs`). N sessions starting together produce N concurrent refresh attempts using the same stored refresh token.
4. **Rotating refresh tokens make the race destructive.** (Inference — consistent with all observed evidence, not provable without vendor logs.) If the authorization server rotates refresh tokens (single-use, common practice), only one concurrent refresh succeeds; the others receive `invalid_grant` → step 2 fires → `clear()` deletes `oauth_creds_<name>`, **wiping the fresh credentials the winning refresh just saved**. Net result: completed auth, then `{}`.

Secondary related fragility, separately verified: all secrets share one JSON blob with read-modify-write on every change (`crates/goose/src/config/base.rs`, `mutate_secrets`), serialized by an in-process mutex only — two goosed processes (e.g. a dev build and a production app) can last-writer-wins clobber each other's saves. We observed this variant too before isolating to a single process.

## Impact

Any user with (a) an installed OAuth-based streamable HTTP extension and (b) anything that creates concurrent sessions — schedules, sub-agents/subrecipes, or simply opening the app while an automation fires — can hit a loop where completed logins are silently destroyed and the browser auth page reappears indefinitely. It presents to users as "this integration never stays logged in."

## Possible directions (non-prescriptive)

- Serialize refresh per extension name (in-process mutex keyed by extension) so concurrent connects share one refresh result.
- Don't clear stored credentials on refresh failures that may be transient/racy (`invalid_grant` from a concurrent rotation, network errors); reserve `clear()` for definitive rejection after a serialized retry.
- Skip the forced refresh when the stored access token is still comfortably valid (rmcp's `get_access_token` already has expiry-aware refresh logic).
- Longer-term: per-key secret entries or cross-process locking for the secrets blob.

---


## Related

- #11084 — Reopening old sessions re-triggers OAuth browser flows for uninstalled MCP extensions. Same symptom family (surprise OAuth browser windows) but a distinct root cause: session resume replays a stale per-session extension snapshot with no reconciliation against installed extensions. The two compound: after this issue wipes `oauth_creds_<name>`, resuming any old chat whose snapshot contains that MCP hits the 401 → browser-auth path even if the user has uninstalled the extension.

items.title: Fine-grained shell permissions: regex-based allow/ask/deny rules for commands under the developer extension's shell tool

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

items.body:
**What problem would this solve?**

goose permissions currently apply to tools as a whole. The developer extension's shell tool can only be set to *Always Allow*, *Ask Before*, or *Never Allow*:

- *Ask Before* on the shell tool: prompts for **every** command, including trivially safe ones like `git status`, `ls`, `cat`, which makes long-running interactive sessions painful and pushes users toward looser settings.
- *Always Allow* (or relying on `smart_approve`'s LLM read-only classification): no deterministic protection against specific command classes: nothing stops a `git push`, a `rm -rf` variant, or a destructive `docker` command that the classifier happens to consider read-only.

The `smart_approve` has two issues:

- the practical issue: false negatives. For example, the LLM deemed fine to reset my git working tree and lost a few hours of work (not in `git reflog` either, because it just got discarded)
- the theoretical issue: the smart_approve runs using the same llm model. If the model is compromised/trained to allow very specific commands even in adversarial mode, that's a security hole. We could run it with another LLM model and that would solve it, although this can get hardware expensive.

This came up in #11017, where I tried to configure exactly this kind of policy (auto-allow `git log`/`git status`, always ask for other `git` commands) using a `permissions:` block with `extension`/`pattern`/`action` entries (that syntax is not supported and is silently ignored). Issue #9407 does somehow duplicate some of this issue, but I wanted to point out the problems with smart_approve here, and refine the issue further.

**What would a good outcome look like?**

Users can define permission rules scoped to a specific tool (starting with the developer extension's shell tool) that match on the tool's arguments — i.e., the shell command string — using regular expressions, with the same three semantics as existing tool permissions:

- **allow** — the command runs without a prompt, even when the `smart_approve` classifier would flag it
- **ask** — a prompt is always shown for matching commands, even when smart_approve would have auto-approved them
- **deny** — the command is never executed; the tool call is rejected with an explanation.

Also, maybe important - when several rules match, the most restrictive action wins (`deny` > `ask` > `allow`)

Goose could also:

- show which rule matched for a prompt
- `goose info` / config tooling can list the rules
- other tools could later expose argument-level rules (e.g., path patterns for the text editor) as well, although shell commands is a priority

Example config for this:

```yaml
tool_permissions:
  developer__shell:
    rules:
      - pattern: '^git\s+(log|status|diff|show)\b'
        action: allow
      - pattern: '^git\s+(push|rebase|reset)\b'
        action: ask
      - pattern: '^\s*(rm\s+-rf\s+/\s*$|mkfs\b|dd\s+if=)'
        action: deny
```

**Possible approaches**

- **Extend the existing tool-permission mechanism** rather than introducing a parallel system: the docs describe per-tool levels managed by `goose configure` (stored in `permission.yaml`, runtime decisions in `permissions/tool_permissions.json`). Adding an optional list of argument-matching rules per tool slots into the existing precedence — explicit tool permissions are already evaluated before the `smart_approve` classifier, which is the behavior the issue thread confirmed is already correct at the tool level.
- **Regex dialect**: use a safe, non-backtracking regex engine (e.g., Rust `regex` crate syntax) to avoid ReDoS from user- or model-supplied patterns, and decide on anchoring semantics (whole-command match vs. search).
- **Compound commands**: rules must be evaluated so they cannot be bypassed by chaining — `git log && git push` should be treated as matching the `git push` rule, not only the `^git\s+log` prefix rule. Per-subcommand evaluation with the most-restrictive-wins rule (point 2 above) handles this naturally; this needs explicit design and tests.
- **Scope**: start with the developer extension's shell tool only, as requested; keep the rule shape tool-generic so other extensions can opt in later.
- **Syntax design**: prior art from Claude Code (`Bash(git log:*)`-style allow/deny rules) is a useful reference for what users in this ecosystem expect.
- **Security behavior**:
   - The agent modifying rules is the big problem. Even if rules are only reloaded per session, not per tool call, an agent could launch another session and exploit modified rules. Maybe there is a way to prevent the agent from modifying without "ask" this rules yaml block from the config, no matter what?
   - Rules evaluation must stay outside LLM control
   - Be explicit in the docs that regex matching is a guardrail, not a sandbox: `bash -c 'git push'`, aliases, and quoting can evade string patterns. The smart_approve can then handle obfuscated commands as well. Hard isolation (containers, filesystem restrictions) is a separate capability.

**Additional context**
 
- Current online documentation:
  - Permission modes: https://goose-docs.ai/docs/guides/managing-tools/goose-permissions (auto / approve / smart_approve / chat; `smart_approve` uses best-effort LLM read/write classification).
  - Tool permissions: https://goose-docs.ai/docs/guides/managing-tools/tool-permissions (per-tool only: Always Allow / Ask Before / Never Allow, via `goose configure`).
- Reported environment: goose 1.45.0, CLI, Alpine Linux container.

- [x] I have verified this does not duplicate an existing feature request - well there is #9407 which has a some similarity.

items.title: docs: add Compartment (encrypted, offline agent memory) to the extensions directory
items.body:
Adds one entry to `documentation/static/servers.json` for Compartment, an open-source (Apache-2.0) MCP server that gives goose a long-term memory that is encrypted at rest and works fully offline.

- One vault file on the user's machine, shared by every MCP client, so what goose learns is available to Claude Code, Cursor or Hermes Agent and back.
- XChaCha20-Poly1305 on every record and vector, Argon2id keyslots, per-record keys (deleting a memory is a crypto-shred), a hash-chained audit log, and a runtime guard that refuses sockets and name lookups.
- Embeddings computed locally with an int8 ONNX model that ships in the package; hybrid vector plus full-text search; importance tiers, expiry dates and supersession.
- 14 tools with titles and read-only or destructive annotations; runs under mcp 1.x and 2.x.

Entry details: `uvx compartment --caller goose serve` (the `--caller` value only labels the client in the vault's audit log). The one-time `uvx compartment init` and the unlock step are stated in `installation_notes`. `is_builtin` and `endorsed` are false, no environment variables.

Links: https://github.com/MaxFreedomPollard/Compartment, PyPI `compartment` 4.9.4 (2026-09-02), official registry `io.github.MaxFreedomPollard/compartment`.

items.title: fix: always run model analysis on recipe scan
items.body: The recipe security scan short circuited to approved when a benign hint matched, and the benign check missed common destructive patterns, so a malicious recipe could skip model analysis. This always runs the model analysis and keeps the hint as metadata only.

items.title: Possible v1.52.0 regression: Goose Desktop loses chat history after restart
items.body:
## Describe the bug

A long-running Goose Desktop conversation disappeared from Goose history after upgrading from v1.51.0 to v1.52.0 and subsequently restarting the application.

The recurring user-visible behavior was first observed after the v1.51.0 → v1.52.0 upgrade on September 23, 2026. The affected conversation belonged to a private Game Boy/Pokémon analysis and automation workspace. It represented milestone work involving Game Boy screen-state understanding through emulated hardware memory and display-state interpretation. Its exact title is no longer known, but it used an internal milestone-style naming pattern similar to `STG-1`.

The conversation is not merely absent from the sidebar. Its canonical session/title record was not found in the active SQLite database or in the preserved database, WAL, SHM, repair, backup, and renderer-state copies examined during recovery.

However, Goose raw provider-request logs still contain substantial context from the missing conversation, including timestamps from the incident date and the correct project workspace. The request payloads do not contain a reliable original Goose session ID or title.

The initial loss event was not captured live, so the exact deletion or persistence failure has not been proven.

## To Reproduce

The following sequence describes the observed failure pattern:

1. Run Goose Desktop on Windows from a desktop shortcut pointing to an unpacked Goose installation.
2. Configure and use a custom OpenAI-compatible provider with a long-running project conversation.
3. Continue using the conversation over an extended period.
4. Upgrade Goose from v1.51.0 to v1.52.0.
5. Close Goose normally and reopen it from the same desktop shortcut.
6. Alternatively, reboot Windows and then reopen Goose.
7. Open the sidebar and Session History.
8. Search for the previously existing long-running conversation.

Observed result:

- The conversation may no longer appear in the sidebar or Session History.
- Repeating close/reopen does not restore it.
- Other conversations may remain available.

Important reproduction limitation:

A controlled close/reopen test performed after the loss did not independently reproduce database deletion. The database remained valid and unchanged across that test. This suggests the original loss may have occurred earlier during concurrent use, database corruption, recovery, migration, or session merging rather than directly during the final shortcut close/reopen operation.

## Expected behavior

Every completed, non-archived conversation should remain recoverable after:

- application upgrade;
- normal application close and reopen;
- Windows reboot and application restart;
- renderer reload;
- backend restart;
- database recovery or migration.

Session History should enumerate all valid sessions, including older sessions and sessions that are not displayed in the recent-chat sidebar.

Session identifiers should remain unique across recovery, migration, restore, and database recreation.

## Screenshots

Not attached. The issue is primarily a persistence and session-enumeration problem.

A private local evidence bundle exists, but it contains project conversation content, database files, renderer state, and provider logs. It is intentionally not attached.

## Please provide the following information

- **OS & Arch:** Windows 11 x64
- **Interface:** Goose Desktop; separate CLI and ACP components were also present
- **Version:** v1.52.0
- **Previous version:** v1.51.0
- **Upgrade date:** September 23, 2026
- **Installation type:** Unpacked Electron/Windows distribution in a custom, nonstandard location; not a conventional installer-managed installation
- **Launcher:** Desktop shortcut with no arguments and an explicit application working directory
- **Extensions enabled:** No extension is required to reproduce the reported persistence behavior; Desktop, CLI, and ACP components may interact with the same session store
- **Provider & Model:** Custom self-hosted OpenAI-compatible provider using a DeepSeek-family model
- **Streaming:** Enabled
- **Session storage:** Local WAL-mode SQLite database under Goose per-user application data

## Additional context

### Possible v1.52.0 regression

The recurring user-visible history-loss behavior began after upgrading Goose from v1.51.0 to v1.52.0.

The upgrade completed successfully using the official Goose release archive. Because the application was an unpacked Electron/Windows tree, the built-in updater refused to update it in place. The application was instead staged, verified, and replaced while preserving user data and configuration.

The updated application launched normally, and the provider and embedded Goose backend passed health checks. However, the investigation also found malformed database copies whose earliest evidence predates the upgrade. Therefore, the current evidence supports a possible v1.52.0 regression or recovery interaction, but does not prove that v1.52.0 created the original corruption.

Please compare v1.51.0 and v1.52.0 specifically for:

- session persistence and commit behavior;
- startup database recovery;
- migration and merge behavior;
- date-based session-ID allocation;
- hidden-session handling;
- Desktop history enumeration;
- WAL/checkpoint behavior after upgrade;
- interaction with unpacked installation layouts.

### Nonstandard installation and update process

Goose was installed as an unpacked Electron/Windows application rather than through a standard Windows installer. The installation contains the application archive, Chromium runtime files, and updater metadata, but is not registered as a normal installed application.

The built-in updater downloaded the official release but refused to update the application in place because the directory did not look like a conventional app-install directory. The application was updated from v1.51.0 to v1.52.0 using a staged replacement of the unpacked tree, with user data and configuration preserved.

This may be relevant because updater, launcher, application-data, and renderer-state assumptions may differ from those used by a standard installation.

### Separate GUI and CLI configuration

The Goose GUI and CLI use separate runtime configuration locations:

- The GUI stores provider/model state under Goose GUI application data and uses a protected keychain field for the API key.
- The CLI uses the Block/Goose application-data location.
- A PowerShell wrapper supplies the CLI provider, model, and API-key environment at launch.
- Desktop, CLI, and ACP/server activity have all been used on the same machine and may access the shared session database.

The custom provider uses:

- Provider ID: `dgx_spark_qwen38`
- Model: `qwen3.8-27b`
- OpenAI-compatible `/v1` API base
- Streaming enabled
- API key entered through Goose’s protected provider field or supplied to the CLI process through the wrapper

The remote inference service and embedded Goose backend passed health checks during the later investigation. The provider was therefore not the only or primary explanation for the missing session.

### Prior provider fallback issue

A separate post-reboot issue could cause Goose to fall back to an older local provider configuration, including an `openai` provider, the `fast` model, and a loopback endpoint.

The relevant stale user-scoped overrides were:
GOOSE_PROVIDER
GOOSE_MODEL
OPENAI_HOST

These were checked independently and should be excluded when testing session persistence. The fallback-provider symptom and the missing-session symptom may be related through restart timing, but they should not be treated as the same failure.

**Database and recovery evidence**
A controlled close/reopen test produced the following results:
- Before close: SQLite integrity_check=ok, 59 sessions, 3,383 messages
- After close: SQLite integrity_check=ok, 59 sessions, 3,383 messages
- After reopening from the Desktop shortcut: SQLite integrity_check=ok, 59 sessions, 3,383 messages
- Embedded backend health endpoint: HTTP 200 with body ok
Other sessions remained available.
The missing session was not found in:
- the active SQLite database;
- WAL and SHM files;
- preserved repair databases;
- database backups;
- renderer-state copies.
Historical repair work also found malformed SQLite copies from the earlier failure period.
Session-ID collision risk
Recovery used date-based identifiers such as:
`YYYYMMDD_N`
After database recreation, newly created sessions reused identifiers that had belonged to older sessions. This created a possible collision or merge risk.
Older sessions were restored from authoritative backup material, and colliding post-recovery sessions were renamed during local recovery. This indicates that recovery and merge logic should not use date-based identifiers as the sole identity key.

**Hidden sessions and renderer limitations**
Some intact sessions used hidden or sub-agent session types and were excluded from normal Desktop history or ACP session/list results.
The renderer/sidebar also requests only a limited recent-session set. Older sessions require explicit history navigation. Goose can additionally reopen on a New Chat route, which can make the application appear empty even when the backend and database still contain sessions.
Non-destructive visible copies of hidden sessions became discoverable after relaunch, confirming that hidden-session filtering can independently cause history to appear missing.
However, resetting renderer state did not restore the critical missing session because its canonical session/title row was absent from the inspected database copies.

**Raw provider logs**
Raw provider-request logs retain approximately 160 deduplicated logged messages and provider-response fragments related to the affected conversation.
The reconstruction is not a restored Goose session. It cannot establish:
- the original Goose session ID;
- the exact original title;
- the complete canonical message sequence.
It does establish that substantial provider activity occurred while the conversation was being used, even though the corresponding canonical Goose session record could not be recovered.

**Local mitigation**
As an operational mitigation, the local CLI launcher wrapper was changed to refuse CLI Goose startup while the unpacked Goose Desktop executable is running against the same session store.
This was intended to prevent overlapping Desktop/CLI writers. The packaged Goose binary itself was not modified.

**Investigation-only diagnostic session**
During investigation, a diagnostics command unintentionally created one hidden diagnostic session containing nine messages. Those records were preserved and are excluded from the claim about the original missing conversation.

**Suspected cause**
The root cause is not proven.
The strongest hypothesis is a combination of:
1. SQLite/WAL instability or lost writes caused by overlapping Desktop, CLI, ACP, or recovery writers;
2. recovery-time session-ID collisions or merges caused by date-based identifiers;
3. hidden-session filtering that prevents valid sessions from appearing in normal history;
4. limited renderer/sidebar enumeration that masks older sessions;
5. possible divergence between GUI, CLI, ACP, and recovered database state.
The controlled close/reopen test argues against the Desktop shortcut directly deleting the database. The evidence instead points toward an earlier persistence, corruption, recovery, or merge failure, followed by UI filtering that made the loss harder to diagnose.

**Requested maintainer investigation**
Please investigate:
- concurrent Desktop/CLI/ACP access to the same SQLite database and WAL;
- connection lifecycle, locking, checkpointing, and WAL recovery behavior;
- whether completed provider requests can succeed without an atomic Goose session commit;
- collision-resistant session identifiers across restore, migration, and recovery;
- recovery merges based on stable identity rather than date-based IDs alone;
- preservation and discoverability of hidden, sub-agent, and older sessions;
- whether Session History queries the authoritative database rather than only a recent-session cache;
- whether orphaned provider-request context can be surfaced as a recoverable session;
- whether unsupported unpacked installation layouts affect update, migration, or data-path behavior.
Please add end-to-end tests covering:
- long-running sessions;
- custom providers;
- application upgrade from v1.51.0 to v1.52.0;
- Desktop close/reopen;
- renderer reload;
- backend restart;
- WAL checkpoint and reopen;
- reboot and relaunch;
- concurrent-client prevention;
- recovery with duplicate-looking session identifiers;
- hidden and sub-agent session visibility;
- verification that every committed session remains discoverable in Session History.
**Related reports**
- [WAL-reset race corrupting sessions.db — #11155](https://github.com/aaif-goose/goose/issues/11155)
- [SQLite connection leak and database locking — #7624](https://github.com/aaif-goose/goose/issues/7624)
- [Custom-provider/ACP session loading behavior — #11370](https://github.com/aaif-goose/goose/issues/11370)
- [Migration-related orphaned sessions — #8638](https://github.com/aaif-goose/goose/issues/8638)
No raw provider logs, reconstructed transcript, database files, renderer state, credentials, authorization headers, usernames, machine names, or absolute local paths are attached.

items.title: fix(security): SmartApprove must not auto-approve tools on server-declared readOnlyHint
items.body:
## Summary

- In SmartApprove mode, the permission inspector short-circuited any tool whose server declared `readOnlyHint: true` straight to `Allow` — no user approval, no LLM judgment.
- The MCP spec designates tool annotations as **untrusted hints** from the server. A malicious or compromised MCP server can mark a destructive tool `readOnlyHint: true` and have goose auto-execute it (delete files, exfiltrate data) while the user believes SmartApprove only auto-runs safe reads.
- Remove the short-circuit: annotated tools now flow through the existing LLM read-only detection like every other tool. Genuinely read-only calls are still auto-approved — but on the model's judgment of the actual call, not the server's self-certification.

## Impact if unsolved

Any third-party MCP server a user connects gets silent auto-execution of arbitrary tools in SmartApprove mode by setting one annotation flag. The write-direction hint (`readOnlyHint: false`) was already distrusted correctly (cached as AskBefore) — the trust asymmetry was only in the direction that reduces security.

## Test plan

- Updated `smart_approve_annotation_defers_to_llm_judge` (was `smart_approve_annotation_allows`): an annotated read-only tool with no cache entry now defers to the LLM judge path instead of blind `Allow`.
- Full `cargo test -p goose --lib permission::` passes (32 tests).

Made with [Cursor](https://cursor.com)

items.title: fix(permissions): enforce manual approval for code mode

- label Code Mode's `execute_bash` tool as mutating, destructive, non-idempotent, and open-world

- add a regression over the tool metadata published by filesystem disclosure mode

## Verification

- `cargo test -p goose execute_bash_annotations_require_approval --features code-mode`
- `cargo test -p goose test_inspect_action --features code-mode` (8 passed)

items.title: Structured per-provider config block, non-destructive provider switching

labels.name: needs_human
labels.description: label to set when a robot looks at a PR and can't handle it

items.body:
## Summary

Switching providers destructively overwrote `GOOSE_PROVIDER` / `GOOSE_MODEL`,
losing the previous provider's settings (#6692). Zero-config ACP providers
(claude-acp, codex-acp, etc.) never got their `_configured` marker set,
so they didn't appear in the model switcher (#8373).

This PR adds a structured `providers:` config block (similar to `extensions:`)
that preserves each provider's model and configured state independently.
An automatic migration converts the old flat-key layout on first load.

**Old format (flat keys, destructive on switch):**
```yaml
GOOSE_PROVIDER: lmstudio
GOOSE_MODEL: qwen/qwen3.6-35b-a3b
claude-acp_configured: true
lmstudio_configured: true
```

**New format (per-provider, non-destructive):**
```yaml
providers:
  claude-acp:
    enabled: true
    model: claude-opus-4-6
    configured: true
  lmstudio:
    enabled: true
    model: qwen/qwen3.6-35b-a3b
    configured: true
  claude-code:
    enabled: true
    model: claude-opus-4-6
    configured: true
active_provider: lmstudio
```

Key changes:
- New `crate::config::providers` module with `ProviderEntry`, read/write helpers, and active-provider accessors
- `get_goose_provider()` / `get_goose_model()` now resolve through the structured block first, falling back to legacy flat keys
- Backend `/config/read` and `/config/upsert` intercept `GOOSE_PROVIDER` / `GOOSE_MODEL` keys so existing frontend code works unchanged
- Resolution order: `GOOSE_PROVIDER` / `GOOSE_MODEL` env vars → `active_provider` / `providers.{name}.model` in config → legacy flat keys in config
- Migration removes stale flat keys (`GOOSE_PROVIDER`, `GOOSE_MODEL`, `*_configured`) on load
- `ProviderDetails` API response includes `saved_model` so the model switcher can pre-populate
- Provider name constants (`TETRATE_PROVIDER_NAME`, etc.) made `pub` to avoid literal string duplication across crates (if you'd prefer a different approach, happy to adjust)
- **Note:** When using the "Switch models" dialog, wait for the model list to settle before completing the provider/model switch

**Questions for maintainers:**

1. `ui/desktop/src/api/types.gen.ts` is committed (not gitignored) but auto-generated by `pnpm run generate-api`. This PR hand-edits it to add `saved_model?` to `ProviderDetails`. Should this be regenerated from the OpenAPI spec instead, and if so, how much of the non-generated `types.gen.ts` content is expected to be hand-maintained? In my experience, generated files typically don't get tracked.

2. This PR only moves `model`, `enabled`, and `configured` into the per-provider block — the minimum needed for non-destructive switching. Are there other per-provider settings (e.g. thinking params, context limits, request params) that should also move to this block?

3. `CUSTOM_DISTROS.md` has config file examples using the old flat-key format (`GOOSE_PROVIDER`, `GOOSE_MODEL`). These still work through the fallback chain, but the examples could be updated to show the new `providers:` / `active_provider:` format. I would be willing to update those references in this PR or a follow-up, whichever you prefer.

### Testing

- Unit tests for `providers.rs` (read/write, fallback chains, multi-provider preservation)
- Unit tests for migration (basic, multi-provider, idempotent, cleanup of stale keys)
- Unit tests for `merge_config_values` with providers block
- Manual testing: installed .deb, verified provider switching preserves settings, migration runs on first load, onboarding screen works

### Related Issues
Fixes #6692
Fixes #8373

items.title: feat(desktop): archive sessions + per-chat sidebar actions
items.body:
Closes #10277. Pin/Star is split out as a distinct follow-up: #10636.

## What

Adds a per-chat **⋯ menu** (hover or right-click) to each session in the sidebar `CHATS` list, exposing **Rename**, **Archive**, and **Delete** — no more detour to Session History for these high-frequency actions.

**Archive** is the net-new capability: a non-destructive hide. Archiving removes a chat from the active sidebar and the Active history list while preserving the record. It stays findable — a keyword search in Session History still surfaces archived matches — and a dedicated **Archived** tab lets you browse and restore.

## Why

Session management was split across two surfaces: the sidebar had only double-click rename, and the only way to declutter it was permanent deletion or waiting for sessions to age out. Archive gives a safe middle ground, and surfacing rename/archive/delete in the sidebar closes a UX gap versus comparable tools.

## How

- **Backend (`crates/goose`)**: new `ArchivedFilter` (`Active`/`Archived`/`All`) added to the session-list query as a SQL `WHERE` clause on the existing `archived_at` column, wired through the ACP `listSessions` `_meta.archived` param and folded into the pagination cursor's filter hash so cursors can't cross filters. Unit test `test_session_list_paged_archived_filter`.
- **Sidebar (`NavigationPanel`)**: reuses the existing Radix `DropdownMenu`; delete goes through the shared `ConfirmationModal`. `useNavigationSessions` listens for `SESSION_ARCHIVED` to drop/refetch rows live.
- **Rename**: `InlineEditText` gains an `editRequestSignal` so the menu can start inline editing programmatically.
- **Session History (`SessionListView`)**: Active/Archived tabs + an archive/restore toggle per card. Active view lists with `archived=all` when a keyword is present so archived sessions remain searchable. The view consumes `SESSION_ARCHIVED`/`SESSION_DELETED`/`SESSION_RENAMED` lifecycle events so it stays in sync with actions taken from the sidebar or other windows.
- **Cross-window consistency (`sessionLifecycleBridge`, `sessionStatusBroadcast`)**: archive/delete events relay through the main process so every window unmounts the affected chat and clears its ACP snapshot; a cross-window busy registry (`useSessionBusyElsewhere`) gates archive/delete on sessions with active runs anywhere, not just the current window.

Sidebar and recent-session lists request `archived=active`, so archived chats are hidden by default everywhere except the Archived tab and keyword search.

## Scope

**Pin/Star is intentionally out of scope** for this PR — it's the only piece of #10277 that needs a new DB column + migration + ACP method, and it's tracked as a follow-up in #10636. This PR delivers the declutter-without-losing capability, which is the core of the request.

## Testing

- `tsc --noEmit` (ui/desktop) — clean
- `cargo test -p goose … test_session_list_paged_archived_filter` — passes
- `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy -p goose --all-targets` — clean
